---
title: "Evaluate Static Capacitance on a View"
subtitle: "Inspect finite C, retained-coordinate reductions, and coordinate entries"
toc-depth: 2
---

The [Static Capacitance Contract](../contracts/static-capacitance.qmd) defines
the candidate API and its failure boundary. `retain()` on a View chooses the
coordinate boundary; `StaticCapacitanceSpec()` chooses the static C equation.
This guide shows the full matrix, a retained reduction, coordinate entries,
and sensitivities at one effective point.

## Evaluate the compiled matrix

Reuse a sealed Plan, its original View or an existing coordinate-transform-only
View, and one effective parameter point. The static matrix is bound to the
same compiled finite model as that request; it includes the finite-pi
capacitance of any discretized transmission line.

```python
from scnsim import StaticCapacitanceSpec

capacitance_spec = StaticCapacitanceSpec()
matrix_result = run.evaluate(
    view,
    capacitance_spec,
    parameters=point,
)
capacitance = matrix_result.matrix.to("farad")
```

The Spec has no `zero_charge` argument. Without a retained View, it returns the
full ordered finite matrix for the selected View, including finite-pi internal
coordinates. The row and column IDs remain usable for static element reads;
they do not become new View coordinates or make internal nodes selectable by
`retain()`.

`matrix_result.row_coordinates` and `matrix_result.column_coordinates` give the
ordered compiled node-coordinate IDs for the two matrix axes. The matrix covers
that complete coordinate basis, including internal non-Port coordinates.
`matrix_result.evidence` binds its Plan, effective parameter point, selected
View, dtype, and finite discretization. This is a capacitance matrix, not a
frequency-indexed response.
The returned row and column IDs, including internal finite-pi axes, can be
used for static element reads. View-retained coordinates themselves remain
limited to the existing public and transform coordinates.

For an existing paired-coordinate View, the runtime resolves its actual
parameter-dependent real transform $T(\theta)$ and evaluates
$C_y=T(\theta)^T C_x(\theta)T(\theta)$. The transformation changes the
coordinate representation; it does not rewire the Plan. A retained View uses
its selected coordinate order and the static C-only zero-charge reduction
described below. A valid PTC lineage may also be used; its resistive/reference
load mask does not change C or transform weights.

## Retain coordinates before evaluating C

Use the same `retain()` View used by the rest of the analysis pipeline. Its
declared coordinate order is the static matrix order; the full finite
complement, including internal finite-pi nodes, is eliminated at zero charge.
The reduction is derived from the View rather than separately entered in the
Spec:

```python
from scnsim import ReductionPipeline, StaticCapacitanceSpec

retained_view = run.original.reduce(
    ReductionPipeline().retain(
        retained_coordinate_a,
        retained_coordinate_b,
    )
)
retained_spec = StaticCapacitanceSpec()
retained_result = run.evaluate(
    retained_view,
    retained_spec,
    parameters=point,
)
effective_capacitance = retained_result.matrix.to("farad")
```

With $r$ denoting the ordered retained coordinates and $e$ their full finite
complement, the static operation uses

$$
C_{\mathrm{eff}}=C_{rr}-C_{re}\,\operatorname{solve}(C_{ee},C_{er}),
\qquad q_e=0.
$$

The result's `zero_charge` field and its evidence retain the actual View-derived
partition and $q_e=0$ condition; it is empty when there is no retained
boundary. This is not a voltage clamp, physical ground, or guessed node. A
singular full matrix may still be exported. If the selected $C_{ee}$ block
cannot be solved, the request reports that native failure; it does not
substitute a pseudoinverse or regularize the block.

## Select one coordinate entry

The `column` keyword is deliberate and names the second matrix axis:

```python
entry_spec = capacitance_spec.element(
    row=row_coordinate,
    column=column_coordinate,
)
entry_result = run.evaluate(view, entry_spec, parameters=point)
entry = entry_result.value.to("farad")
```

The element result preserves `row`, `column`, and the same
Plan/point/View/discretization provenance as a matrix result. Select row and
column IDs from the result axes of the View being evaluated; for a retained
View, these are the retained axes. A full-matrix internal coordinate ID can
address a full-view element, but is not a new retain handle.

To select an entry after a retained-matrix evaluation, use its retained row and
column IDs with the same retained View:

```python
retained_row_id = retained_result.row_coordinates[0]
retained_column_id = retained_result.column_coordinates[0]
retained_entry_spec = retained_spec.element(
    row=retained_row_id,
    column=retained_column_id,
)
retained_entry_result = run.evaluate(
    retained_view,
    retained_entry_spec,
    parameters=point,
)
```

## Differentiate the same matrix or element

For sensitivities, use the selector on the same View and the same effective
point. For example, a Jacobian differentiates each matrix entry with respect to
the ordered physical parameter list:

```python
from scnsim import Jacobian, SensitivitySpec

sensitivity_spec = SensitivitySpec(
    quantities={"C": retained_spec.matrix.on(retained_view)},
    wrt=(capacitance_parameter,),
    derivative=Jacobian(),
    discretization=fixed_mesh,
)
jacobian_result = run.sensitivity(
    sensitivity_spec,
    parameters=point,
)
```

For an element, bind `retained_entry_spec.value.on(retained_view)` as the
quantity instead. The existing JVP and VJP declarations work on either
selected quantity. Their directions and weights follow the ordinary
physical-unit rules in the
[Sensitivity guide](sensitivity.qmd); the static-C outputs have units of
farads. A raw matrix Jacobian therefore has units F per SI unit of the input;
when the input is itself measured in F, the cell is dimensionless by unit
cancellation, not by automatic sensitivity normalization. Derivatives pass
through the parameter-dependent $C(\theta)$, resolved $T(\theta)$, and the
actual elimination solve. The transform weights are not replaced by baseline
constants.

Use one fixed realized finite mesh for the sensitivity request. A valid PTC
lineage is supported, but the PTC resistive/reference load mask has no
numerical effect on C or transform weights; this static request does not apply
RF/Port eligibility or normalization. The derivative
does not differentiate an integer line-section choice. Static capacitance uses the shared JAX physical program.

Memory and Workspace results expose the same static matrix and element value
interfaces. Memory results are detached; Workspace results use fixed selected
readers and may be inspected after `run.close()`. The dynamic response, root,
and residue-normalized-coupling contracts remain separate.

The dev36 retained-View static equation is newly integrated and its numerical
use has not yet been observed. Prior dev35 static LC observations do not verify
this retained request path. The existing dynamic `retain()` equation remains
unchanged: it uses its dynamic Schur behavior, including the zero-external-
current boundary, while this static quantity eliminates only C under
$q_e=0$.
